newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico drug lord probably died amid bawling babies.
newsitem.headline: Mexico drug lord probably died amid bawling babies.

text.p: After life as a playboy billionaire playing cat-and-mouse with the law, one of the world's leading cocaine lords likely spent his last hours in a hospital surrounded by expectant mothers and wailing newborns.

Amado Carrillo Fuentes apparently died not in a showdown with the many U.S. and Mexican drug agents who pursued him for nearly a decade but of a heart attack after undergoing plastic surgery and liposuction.
The Attorney General's Office has not yet confirmed his death, saying they were not completely sure of the corpse's identity because of the extensive plastic surgery.
Carrillo's family said the drug baron, believed to be 42, died on Friday in Mexico City's small Santa Monica Hospital, which until recently catered exclusively to pregnant women.

"It is not the nicest hospital in the city," said Rodrigo Diez, a 25-year-old computer consultant standing at his office in front of the hospital. "Mostly women go in there because the tradition stuck from when it was just for maternity."

No one on the quiet, tree-lined street in the upper-class Polanco district could testify to seeing the reclusive drug lord enter the hospital. "He couldn't have called a lot of attention to himself because the guard at the building facing the hospital didn't notice anything special," Diez said.
The last clear photograph of Carrillo, who often wore disguises, was taken about eight years ago although he was videotaped at his sister's wedding earlier this year.

Carrillo got his nickname as "Lord of the Skies" from his tactic of flying cocaine in old commercial planes to northern Mexico from Colombia for shipment to the United States. He had almost finished building a fantasy palace in Hermosillo in Sonora state, just a few blocks from the homes of the state governor and the U.S. consul.
He was the subject of 26 investigations by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency, which described him as "the most powerful figure in the Mexican drug trade."
